The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce has urged the Government to ensure that proposed security legislation incorporates clear legal definitions, adequate judicial oversight and due process safeguards, and warning that legal certainty is important to investor confidence and Sri Lanka’s continued access to the European Union’s GSP+ trade concession.

In a statement issued yesterday, the Chamber noted it had submitted its observations on the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA) and was finalising its views on the proposed Prevention of Organised Crime Act, which would be communicated to the relevant authorities shortly.

Whilst recognising the Government’s efforts to strengthen national security and address emerging challenges, the Chamber has called for a careful review of the draft legislation to ensure that security objectives are balanced with safeguards necessary to maintain a predictable, rules-based business environment.

It added that clear legal provisions and appropriate oversight were essential to preserving investor confidence, legal certainty and Sri Lanka’s reputation as a destination for trade and investment.

The Chamber also highlighted the importance of maintaining Sri Lanka’s access to the EU’s GSP+, which supports exports, employment, foreign exchange earnings and economic growth.

It urged the Government to ensure that new legislation remained aligned with Sri Lanka’s international commitments and internationally accepted standards, noting that this would strengthen the country’s prospects of retaining GSP+ benefits.

“The Ceylon Chamber remains committed to constructive engagement with policymakers and other stakeholders to ensure that legislative reforms effectively address national priorities while supporting economic growth, competitiveness, and sustainable development,” it stated.

Officers of the Narcotics Control Unit (NCU) of Sri Lanka Customs carried out the largest-ever pill seizure in Sri Lanka at Katunayake, arresting a 46-year-old Indian national at Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA) on Wednesday (28), after finding cocaine and ecstasy with an estimated street value of Rs. 454 million in his luggage.

The suspect, an engineer by profession, had arrived in Sri Lanka from Paris via Doha on Qatar Airways flight QR 654. NCU officers stopped him at the airport for further examination.

During a search of his luggage, officers found suspicious substances that were later identified as cocaine and ecstasy.

The haul included about 5,121 grams of cocaine, with an estimated street value of Rs. 256 million. Officers also seized 13,173 grams of ecstasy, equivalent to roughly 23,000 tablets, valued at about Rs. 198 million, making this the largest pill seizure ever recorded in the country. Together, the narcotics are worth an estimated Rs. 454 million.

Sri Lanka Customs conducted preliminary investigations following the detection. The suspect, along with the seized narcotics and other relevant productions, will be handed over to the Police Narcotics Bureau (PNB) for further investigations and legal proceedings.

title: President’s FDI Envoy charts priorities for inclusive growth | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 30 October 2026 00:25
-     - 154

President’s Special Envoy for Foreign Direct Investment and Western Province Governor Hanif Yusoof

– Pic by Shehan Gunasekara

President’s Special Envoy for Foreign Direct Investment and Western Province Governor Hanif Yusoof has said Sri Lanka has for far too long failed to connect its talent and ambition with the opportunities they deserve. He set out what the country needs to build an inclusive economy that draws local and international capital.

Outlining the Government’s commitment to inclusive finance and to creating an environment for capital to grow, Yusoof told the Orange Economy Summit 2026 in Colombo on Wednesday that Sri Lanka lacked neither ambition nor opportunity. He described the country’s greatest natural resource as its people, not its land, forests or location.

The country had come through one of the most difficult periods in its economic history, he said, with a financial crisis and uncertainty that affected almost every household. 

“Recovery alone is not enough. We must build a better economy, a fairer economy, a more inclusive economy,” Yusoof said. That meant an economy where a person’s future is determined by talent and hard work rather than background and circumstances.

Yusoof pointed to one of the economy’s starkest gaps: only about a third of working-age women participate in the labour force, compared with a higher proportion of men. While the country discusses how to attract billions of dollars in foreign investment, he said, a significant part of its own women’s potential remains underutilised. The same holds for young entrepreneurs in rural villages, persons with disabilities and small businesses that could become international exporters if they had access to finance, technology and markets. 

“These are not people without potential. They are people without sufficient opportunity,” he said.

The Government’s most important goal, Yusoof said, is to create the connection between business and society. That requires encouraging education, improving digital connectivity, strengthening transparency and creating an environment where local and international investors can operate with confidence. He identified opportunities in tourism, small industries, agriculture, services, technology and entrepreneurship.

“We must also recognise that climate resilience is now an economic necessity,” Yusoof said. Cyclone Ditwah had shown how quickly livelihoods, infrastructure and years of progress could be lost, he said, and investment must also protect communities and future generations.

Sri Lanka should aim to become a regional centre for inclusive and sustainable investment, Yusoof said, attracting international capital to support small businesses, climate-resilient enterprises and emerging sectors. Linking impact investment with capital market institutions, including the Colombo Stock Exchange, could open new pathways for international capital to reach promising Sri Lankan businesses. As Special Envoy, he said, he saw his role as helping bring investment and opportunity together.

Coming from business, Yusoof said, he understood that financial returns matter. But investors must also ask what difference their capital makes to people’s lives, including whether it creates jobs and empowers women. Financial returns and social impact, he said, need not compete. 

“We do not simply need more capital. We need that capital to reach the right people, create real opportunity and produce lasting value,” he said.

The Government cannot achieve this alone, Yusoof said. Banks, financial institutions, universities, private companies and development partners must work together and move from discussion to action. He said success, judged five years from now, should be measured not by the partnerships signed but by the women who have become entrepreneurs and professionals, the enterprises that have entered international markets and the jobs created.

title: Corporate Bond market too shallow to carry 7% growth: IIX | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 30 October 2026 00:22
-     - 188

IIX Senior Director Priyank Tiwari                            

          – Pic by Shehan Gunasekara

Sri Lanka’s corporate Bond market, at about 1% of GDP, is too shallow to finance the private sector-led growth the country needs to sustain about 7% annual expansion to 2030, according to new research by the Impact Investment Exchange (IIX).

Presenting the report, ‘Financing Sri Lanka’s Inclusive Growth’, at the Orange Economy Summit 2026 in Colombo on Wednesday, IIX Senior Director Priyank Tiwari said the 7% target was almost double the current growth rate, alongside an ambition to double exports.

“Public investment has been at a very steady 3% of GDP, so growth has to come from the private sector, especially when we are talking about high growth targets,” Tiwari said.

Sri Lanka has a strong and stable banking base, he said, and the sector has been undergoing a solid recovery that should allow it to unlock more capital. 

“But the banking sector alone is not enough to fuel this growth,” he said. The CSE’s GSS+ framework has already drawn 12 Bonds, yet the corporate Bond market remains about 1% of GDP. The report argues for systematically deepening Sri Lanka’s financial markets so more companies and institutions can raise capital through different avenues.

The report identifies anchor value chains that are integral to growth, each with its own capital needs. It argues that inclusion runs through these value chains, through the jobs, communities and women they sustain. Strengthening them down to the last mile was essential to meeting the growth and export targets, Tiwari said.

“The starting point for us is not zero,” Tiwari said, citing the Central Bank’s sustainable finance roadmap and taxonomy, the CSE’s GSS+ framework and existing initiatives to improve financing for women entrepreneurs. The task now, he said, was to link these initiatives so the market developed in an integrated manner and in line with global standards.

The report draws on markets where IIX’s model is already operating. In Indonesia, a State-owned anchor issuer, regulatory incentives and a supportive policy environment have moved the market to scale and adoption. Bangladesh saw its first issuance earlier this year and has integrated Orange standards into its GSS guidelines.

title: Clarity, confidence and courage: Helping Sri Lanka’s graduates into work | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 30 October 2026 00:18
-     - 64

For over 30 years, much of my work has involved helping people make sense of where they are in their careers and where they might go next. I have worked with people of different ages, in very different sectors and in different parts of the world. But there is something particularly troubling about what I am seeing amongst young graduates in Sri Lanka today.

These are not young people who have failed to try. Many have done exactly what was expected of them. They worked hard for their O/Ls and A/Ls. Their families paid for tuition and made sacrifices. They competed for university places and earned their degrees. The understanding was that, somewhere at the end of all this effort, there would be a job.

For far too many, that job is simply not there.

The figures tell us just how serious the problem has become. An IMF analysis published in September put unemployment among Sri Lankans aged 15–24 with post-secondary education at around 43%, the highest amongst the 12 Asia-Pacific economies compared. Our own Labour Force Survey measures this differently, but the picture is hardly reassuring. Youth unemployment stood at 19.5%, rising to 22.5% amongst young people with GCE A/L and above. Nearly 40,000 graduates aged 20 and above were unemployed, and around half of them were Arts graduates.

So I think we need to be careful about telling young people that they simply need to become more “employable”. There is a shortage of jobs. The World Bank estimates that nearly one million young Sri Lankans will enter the labour market over the next decade, while, without stronger growth and private investment, only around 300,000 new formal jobs are expected to be created.

We cannot coach our way out of that.

But there is another part of this which I believe we need to talk about. Have we prepared our young people for a world of work that no longer works in the way many of us were brought up to expect?

For generations the pathway was fairly straightforward: Education → Qualification → Job → Career. You did your part and expected the system to do its part.

But now, that relationship has changed.  Careers today are much less tidy. Young people may have to experiment, learn, adapt, reskill, make connections, change direction and try again. Sometimes more than once. I do not think we have done enough to prepare them for that reality.

There is also something particularly Sri Lankan in this. For many students, the subject they study at university is determined by Z-scores and district cut-off marks rather than by their interests, aptitude or career goals. So a young person can spend years earning a degree they did not really choose, and then arrive at the end without ever having had the chance to ask: What am I actually good at? Where could I use it?

In my work I keep coming back to three things: Clarity, Confidence and Courage.

Clarity, for me, is not simply deciding what job you want. It is knowing yourself well enough to understand what you are good at, what gives you energy, what matters to you and where those things might be useful. A degree tells us what somebody studied. It does not tell us all of that.

I think we have put far too much weight on qualifications in Sri Lanka. The right results. The right degree. The right title. Somewhere along the way, the person themselves can get lost.

I remember talking to one young person in Sri Lanka about strengths. Part-way through the conversation they stopped me, genuinely surprised. It had never occurred to them that you could actually enjoy what you do and come away from work energised rather than drained. Work, in their mind, was something you secured and then endured.

That conversation has stayed with me.

Confidence is another matter. Rejection wears people down. So does sending application after application and hearing nothing at all. After a while, a young person can move from thinking “the job market is difficult” to “perhaps I am not good enough”. Those are two very different conclusions.

When I work with people who have reached that point, I often ask them to tell me their story. What have you actually done? What difficulties have you overcome? What have other people trusted you to do? We put it down on paper. Quite often they are surprised by what is there, because they have become so focused on what has gone wrong that they have stopped seeing what has gone right.

Confidence has to come from what we have actually done. Full stop.

And then there is courage. Not dramatic courage. The ordinary kind. Applying for something when you do not meet every criterion. Asking somebody for an introduction. Learning something new when you are worried you might not be very good at it. Taking a first job that does not have the title your family hoped for. Or sometimes seeing a need and creating an opportunity rather than waiting for somebody to offer one.

A couple of years ago I worked with a young Sri Lankan man who was very capable but had become stuck and was being overlooked for promotion. We went through his skills and experience and practised how he could talk about what he had to offer. At his next appraisal, instead of simply waiting to hear what his manager thought of him, he talked about things he could see needed improving in the organisation and how he could help.

His manager listened. A position was created for him to do exactly that.

I like that story because it was not about somebody suddenly becoming fearless. He had become clearer about what he could offer, confident enough to say it, and courageous enough to put an idea on the table. So perhaps, sometimes, instead of only asking “Where is the position?”, we should also be asking “What could I create?”

But I do not want this to turn into yet another lecture to young people about resilience. Confidence and courage cannot manufacture jobs. Employers have a part to play. Universities have a part to play. Policymakers certainly do. And families do too.

Employers can create genuine entry-level opportunities and stop expecting young applicants to arrive with years of experience. Universities can start career conversations in the first year rather than waiting until students are about to leave. Policymakers need to keep working on the much bigger issue of job creation and the connection between education, vocational training and industry. And as families, perhaps we need to loosen our ideas about what a “good” career is supposed to look like.

After more than three decades of doing this work, I have no doubt that the talent is here. Our young people are capable and qualified. What worries me is how many have had very little opportunity to discover what they are good at, where they might contribute, and how much more they are than the certificate they hold.

We cannot promise them certainty and I am not sure we should even try. But we can help them find enough clarity to see a direction, enough confidence to recognise what they already bring, and enough courage to take the next step when the whole route is not yet visible.

The full article, including the supporting data, research and practical recommendations, is available on the Oxford Psychometrics website: oxford-psychometrics.com/qualified-but-uncertain-clarity-confidence-and-courage-for-sri-lankas-young-graduates

(The author is a Chartered Occupational and Coaching Psychologist, Founder of Oxford Psychometrics, and a Registered Career Development Professional with the Career Development Institute (UK), with over three decades of experience in international talent and career development)

title: IDB Launches ‘i5 | FIVE Industry Excellence Journey & Awards 2026’ | Daily FT

The Industrial Development Board (IDB), operating under the Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry, has commenced accepting applications for the ‘i5 | FIVE Industry Excellence Journey & Awards 2026’, a national initiative aimed at recognising and promoting excellence in Sri Lanka’s manufacturing sector.

The program seeks to enhance productivity, innovation, competitiveness and sustainability among local manufacturers while creating opportunities for manufacturing enterprises across the country to improve their performance and prepare for the future of industry. Small, medium and large-scale manufacturing enterprises are invited to apply for this national initiative.

The ‘i5’ program goes beyond a conventional awards ceremony, offering a continuous journey towards industrial excellence and transformation. It is designed around the concept of Industry 5.0, which integrates technological advancement, human capabilities, resilience and sustainable growth to build a more competitive and future-ready manufacturing sector.

A key feature of the initiative is the development of case studies and videos documenting the success stories of award-winning enterprises. These will help share knowledge, practical experience and best practices with other entrepreneurs, encouraging continuous improvement and innovation across the manufacturing sector.

The assessment process will be conducted under three main pillars: Enterprise Excellence, Industry Excellence and Transformation Capability.

Enterprise Excellence focuses on leadership, financial and organisational performance, and stakeholder management. Industry Excellence evaluates manufacturing processes, automation, innovation, operational efficiency, digital capabilities and environmental sustainability. Transformation Capability assesses technology adoption, human resource development, the ability to respond to challenges and long-term sustainable impact.

The programme covers 21 assessment areas across these three pillars, with a total of 69 awards to be presented to enterprises in the small, medium and large-scale categories.

Who can apply? Small, medium and large-scale manufacturing enterprises registered in any district of Sri Lanka and engaged in active manufacturing operations for at least three years are eligible to apply. Micro-scale enterprises are not eligible for this programme.

Applicants will be evaluated through an assessment process that includes the examination of financial records, employee numbers and inspections of manufacturing premises, along with other relevant criteria.

Applications for the program are entirely free of charge. Eligible enterprises must complete and submit their applications online through the official website: www.ifive.idb.lk. The deadline for online applications is Monday, 9 November 2026, at 4.00 p.m.

The National Chamber of Exporters of Sri Lanka (NCE) reviewed sectoral issues, export-market requirements and overseas trade plans at its Council meeting on 20 October 2026. Held in partnership with Prime Group and Melwa at the Prime Marina Sales Suite in Port City, the meeting considered matters the Chamber is taking up with authorities.

The Council reviewed issues being pursued with Government institutions.

Among the matters discussed was the delay in implementing the Madrid Protocol. WIPO›s Madrid System provides trademark holders with a one-stop solution to secure and manage brand protection and covers 117 members representing 133 countries and over 80% of global trade, with more than 1.7 million registered trademarks. According to NIPO, the final draft is now to be submitted to Parliament for approval.

The Council also discussed restrictions affecting the forest sector, and difficulties faced by electrical and electronic product exporters. During January-August 2026, Sri Lanka›s Electrical and Electronic Components (EEC) exports grew exceptionally, by 57.49% YoY to $ 440.31 million. For August 2026 alone, sector earnings reached $ 62.4 million, supported by a 30.83% rise in Insulated Wires and Cables. Overall, this performance highlights the industry›s expanding competitiveness and export potential.

The NCE has been following up with the relevant authorities on these issues, including seeking a documented action plan from the Environment Ministry.

It has also requested further support from the Sri Lankan Commercial Officer in India in addressing trade difficulties arising from India›s BIS-QCOs and discussions with the Inland Revenue Department on VAT refunds are also being pursued.

Changes to import procedures and new European Union regulations were mentioned in the meeting›s review of trade-related concerns. Following Customs› shift to digital processing of import documentation on 1 October, the NCE is surveying exporters to identify difficulties with importing raw materials, machinery, packaging materials and other inputs.

NCE and other stakeholders are seeking technical assistance and training for exporters preparing to help Sri Lankan exporters comply with regulations, including EU›s new limits on mineral oil contaminants (MOAH) in food and agricultural products, due to take effect in January 2027. The EU›s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation was also discussed, given its implications for exporters supplying that market.

At the next sectoral discussions, members will address mineral-based products, chemicals, engineering, and electrical and electronic products.

Topics include supply-chain bottlenecks, tariff barriers under bilateral free trade agreements, standardisation and raw-material costs.

Conducting a presentation on ‘Export and Beyond’, entrepreneur, Chartered Engineer, inventor and KIK Group of Companies Founder and Chairman Lalith Kahatapitiya called for new foreign-exchange channels beyond existing sources. He emphasised the importance of several measures for the economy, including re-exports, local suppliers serving exporters, and the need for a new National Business Facilitation Centre.

The Chamber’s overseas programs are also taking shape, a visit to Italy and Sweden is planned for March 2027, with a trade show in Milan and business meetings in Stockholm. The council also discussed several upcoming plans, such as the NCE Budget Forum on 19 November and the 34th NCE Export Awards on 11 December are also approaching.

The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has urged the Government to substantively redraft the Protection of the State from Terrorism (PSTA) Bill before enactment. It warned that the proposed law reproduces and expands several shortcomings of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) it is meant to replace.

In comments dated 13 October, 2026 on the Bill as gazetted on 22 September, 2026, the OHCHR welcomed the Government’s stated intention to repeal the PTA and acknowledged improvements on the December 2025 draft. The current Bill narrows the definition of terrorism, removes confessions to police as admissible evidence, and provides some safeguards for journalism, research, civil society activity and dissent. It also requires audio-visual recording of police interviews, shortens notification of detention to the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka to 48 hours and establishes a central database of arrests and case outcomes.

“The PSTA Bill still contains multiple provisions that risk contravening the State’s obligations under international human rights law and domestic constitutional guarantees, and carries risks of continuation and recurrence of serious human rights violations observed recurrently under the existing PTA regime,” the OHCHR said.

The Office said the definition of terrorism remains overly broad and vague. It objected to the Bill covering acts committed ‘knowingly’ as well as intentionally, to the undefined phrase ‘unduly compelling a government’, and to the inclusion of harms such as substantial economic loss. Safeguards for protest, advocacy, dissent, strikes and humanitarian aid are framed only as an evidential caution rather than an express exclusion, it said.

Speech-related offences, including inducement to terrorism and dissemination of terrorist publications, contain vague terms and fall below the threshold required for incitement offences, the OHCHR said. Because these offences would apply extraterritorially, they could criminalise lawful expression by people abroad, including members of diaspora communities. The definition of ‘confidential information’ could expose journalists and civil society to prosecution for routine reporting on raids, arrests or checkpoints, it added.

Administrative detention remains central to the framework, the Office said. The Secretary to the Ministry of Defence could order detention for up to two months at a time, up to a maximum of one year, and a Magistrate presented with an initial Detention Order must give effect to it. “The UN Human Rights Committee has noted that such detention presents severe risks of arbitrary deprivation of liberty,” it said. The Bill also makes remand mandatory even where no Detention Order is presented, with a maximum remand period of one year. The Independent Review Committee only makes recommendations, with the Minister of Defence taking the final decision.

The OHCHR raised concern over arrest and search powers extended to the armed forces and coast guard. Suspects they arrest may be held for up to 24 hours before transfer to police, without express guarantees of immediate access to counsel, medical examination or recording of questioning. The Bill does not define chains of command for joint police-military operations, it said, risking gaps in accountability.

It also criticised the breadth of executive powers. These include the President’s power to proscribe organisations without automatic expiry or independent review, and to issue directions on the Act’s implementation without Parliamentary scrutiny. “Immunity provisions should not shield unlawful arrest, torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance, recklessness, gross negligence or other serious human rights violations,” the Office said.

While section 72 would repeal the PTA, section 73 would preserve pending PTA cases, existing regulations and proscriptions. “Repeal should therefore be effective and comprehensive in substance as well as in form, with transitional arrangements reviewed to ensure that no person remains subject to proceedings, detention, evidentiary rules, proscriptions or regulations that are incompatible with international human rights law,” it said.

Among its recommendations, the OHCHR called for the Government to: narrow the definition of terrorism; require prompt, independent judicial oversight of every arrest and detention; make judicial warrants the rule for searches; ensure civilian police primacy; narrow the immunity provisions; and hold meaningful public consultation with civil society, independent institutions and legal experts before further legislative action. The Office said it stood ready to continue its dialogue with the Government and provide technical assistance.

title: Regenerating Colombo: Is adequate housing really for all? | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 30 October 2026 00:25
-     - 47

What does regeneration mean?

On 31 October, World Cities Day 2026 will focus on “Regenerating the City: Adequate Housing for All.” For Colombo, the theme raises a central question: has the city merely grown and modernised—or is it actually regenerating?

Colombo has more homes, improved services, comparatively stronger infrastructure and increasingly valuable land. Yet these achievements do not automatically make the city more affordable, inclusive, accessible or resilient. Regeneration means renewing the connected systems of housing, neighbourhoods, infrastructure, ecology, mobility and opportunity—so that the people who live and work in the city share in the value created by urban change.

The test is therefore not whether Colombo is becoming bigger and more valuable, but whether it is becoming better to live in—and better able to support the people who depend on it.

Colombo’s housing transformation

Colombo District has experienced remarkable housing progress. Occupied housing increased from approximately 272,000 units in 1981 to 654,000 in 2024. By 2024, 98.6% of houses were permanent, 97.2% had drinking water within the unit, 98% had national-grid electricity, and 95.5% had exclusive sanitary facilities. 85.5% of households used LP gas.

Housing is also becoming more intensive: single-storey houses account for 54.4%, multi-storey houses 32.1% and apartments 13.4%. Between 2012 and 2024, total housing units rose from approximately 634,000 to 768,000, while occupied units increased from 556,000 to 654,000.

Colombo has moved beyond simply producing more dwellings. The next challenge is ensuring that homes are affordable, well located, suitable, and connected to jobs and services.

More housing, greater pressure

The growing stock has created a paradox. Between 2012 and 2024, total housing units increased by 21.1%, occupied units by 17.7%, but vacant or permanently closed units by 45.8%—from 78,052 to 113,837. Their share rose from 12.3% to 14.8% (Figure 1).

The question is therefore whether supply matches effective demand—in price, location, tenure and suitability. An earlier Western Province analysis estimated that Colombo alone could have had approximately 101,600 excess or vacant units by 2015, partly linked to investment demand and second or third homes.

Greater density does not automatically mean greater affordability. National HIES evidence shows housing expenditure represented 26.67% of non-food expenditure among Colombo District households in 2019. Rising land values and construction costs have increased the entry cost for first-time buyers and put pressure on low- and middle-income households. Formal finance can assist those with income and credit access, but may widen exclusion.

Internationally, adequate housing includes security of tenure, services, affordability, habitability, accessibility, suitable location and cultural adequacy. Colombo has improved physical housing conditions, but affordability, location, and access to opportunity remain under pressure.

Land values intensify the pressure

The CBSL Residential Land Valuation Index for Colombo District, with 2017 H1 = 100, rose from 176.3 in 2021 to 221.0 in 2023 H2, 242.9 in 2024 H2, 273.1 in 2025 H2 and 284.9 in 2026 H1—placing the latest index 184.9% above its 2017 H1 base (Figure 2).

As land becomes more valuable, households face difficult choices: pay more, accept smaller or denser housing, or move farther from the city. Moving outward may reduce housing costs, but it can increase commuting time, transport expenditure, and distance from employment, services, and opportunity.

This is not merely an affordability issue. It is a regeneration issue. A city cannot be regenerative if economic growth raises land values while displacing people who depend on the city for employment and daily life. Housing can become more valuable as an investment for those who can afford it, while becoming less affordable as a home for those who need it most.

Adequate housing beyond the front door

Adequate housing does not end at the front door. Location, public space, green-blue infrastructure, services, access to employment and the conditions of daily life all determine whether a home supports a decent urban life.

Colombo has made progress in parks, recreation and the use of wetlands as public assets. More than 20 km of walkways and jogging paths have been developed around Colombo’s wetlands. The Colombo Municipal Council provides 32 city playgrounds, 33 children’s playgrounds and 52 community centres.

Yet provision is not the same as access. Evidence indicates that 373 of 557 Grama Niladhari divisions had no public playground within the division, while 73 were 5 km or more away. For children’s parks, 420 divisions had no facility within the division, with 145 located 5 km or more away. Colombo can therefore expand its overall stock of facilities while neighbourhood-level access remains uneven.

A study of Colombo city’s 47 wards found that green cover declined from 35.67% in 1956 to 22.23% in 2010—a reduction of 13.44 percentage points. Colombo is also becoming more vulnerable to flooding: a recent assessment classified 13.64% of the study area as extremely high flood hazard, with built-up land accounting for approximately 85.6%, compared with 6.5% wetlands and 3.7% tree cover. The Colombo Wetland Complex has declined from approximately 47.5 km² in the 1980s to about 19 km² today.

These figures do not mean that urbanisation alone explains flooding. They do show why natural water-retention areas, expanding impervious surfaces and drainage pressure must be treated as housing and urban-planning concerns—not merely environmental issues. Wetlands and vegetation help protect homes, roads, livelihoods and public investment

Residents, merchants, shopkeepers, property owners, institutions and local authorities should be regarded as partners in maintaining and improving urban precincts. Cleaner streets, shaded walkways, greener commercial areas, pocket parks and well-maintained public spaces can become shared assets. A regenerative city therefore requires collective responsibility, not municipal action alone.

International experience offers concise lessons. Melbourne uses neighbourhood-level urban-forest planning and community participation, while Singapore links parks, waterways and nature corridors with precinct partnerships and shared stewardship. These models should be adapted to Colombo’s own environmental, institutional and social conditions rather than copied mechanically.

Mobility adds another dimension. A lower-cost home farther from employment may reduce housing costs but increase transport expenditure, commuting time and the time available for family and community life. Workforce Mobility Management (WMM) makes this relationship visible: the true cost of housing includes the time and money required to reach work, education, healthcare and essential services.

Adequate homes need adequate neighbourhoods—green, clean, connected, accessible and environmentally resilient.

Is Colombo becoming regenerative?

The evidence is mixed. Colombo has improved housing quality, basic services, infrastructure, public spaces and parts of its wetland system. But rising land values, vacant housing, affordability pressures and unequal access to neighbourhood facilities show that regeneration is not benefiting every part of urban life.

The pattern is therefore uneven regeneration. Buildings and infrastructure are improving faster than affordability, access, environmental recovery and social inclusion.

Regeneration must also protect livelihoods. Shops, vendors, carts and other activities may sometimes need relocation for valid reasons such as safety, congestion or planned land use. However, the process should be transparent, reduce hardship, provide workable alternatives and apply rules fairly. Urban improvement should not cause avoidable loss of livelihood. Housing affordability also depends on location. A cheaper home farther from employment may reduce the initial housing cost but increase transport expenses and commuting time. The real housing burden includes land, house price, rent, finance, transport, and time. This connects housing and location with Workforce Mobility Management (WMM). Moving economic activity away from viable locations can also move people farther from their sources of income.

The deeper issue is whether urban growth creates public value. A regeneration dividend should mean affordable housing, better use of vacant units, lower travel costs, fair access to public space, restored wetlands, lower flood risk and protected livelihoods. What is not measured is unlikely to be protected or improved

On this basis, Colombo is regenerating—but unevenly. A regeneration dividend should be visible in affordable housing, better use of vacant units, lower travel costs, fair access to public space, restored wetlands, lower flood risk and protected livelihoods.”

Colombo’s next agenda

Colombo need not choose between development and regeneration. The challenge is to make development itself regenerative—creating economic value while improving housing, neighbourhoods, environmental quality and access to opportunity.

Put affordability at the centre of planning: Consider land values, rents, construction costs, household incomes and finance together.

Use existing housing better: Expand affordable rental options and return suitable vacant units to productive use.

Connect housing, land use and mobility: Measure not only dwelling price but also the time and cost of reaching employment, education and essential services.

Regenerate neighbourhoods and livelihoods, not just buildings: Integrate housing investment with transport, drainage, sanitation, public spaces and green-blue infrastructure, while recognising the locations on which small businesses and daily-income activities depend.

Make regeneration participatory: Residents, merchants, property owners, businesses, institutions and local authorities should share responsibility for creating cleaner, greener and better-maintained precincts. Residents should be partners in shaping and sustaining regeneration, not merely its beneficiaries.

Cities must change, and redevelopment will sometimes be necessary. But change should be strategic, transparent and inclusive—improving the urban environment without unnecessary displacement and providing viable pathways for livelihoods to adapt.

Colombo’s next chapter should not be judged by how much the city builds, but by how well it regenerates.

title: A Buddhist perspective on environmental law | Daily FT
summary:

Executive Summary

Buddhism, originating in India between the fifth and fourth centuries BCE and founded by Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, offers a comprehensive ethical framework that extends beyond spiritual liberation (Nirvana) to encompass social, legal, and ecological responsibility. Central to Buddhist philosophy are the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path, which emphasise ethical conduct (sila), mental discipline (samadhi), and wisdom (pañña) as the foundations of harmonious living. These principles cultivate compassion (karuna), loving-kindness (metta), non-harm (ahimsa), mindfulness (sati), and interdependence (paticca-samuppada), all of which have profound implications for environmental protection and sustainability. This article examines how Buddhist ethical teachings can inform and reshape contemporary environmental law by challenging anthropocentric legal paradigms and promoting ecocentric, relational, and responsibility-based approaches to environmental governance. Through doctrinal analysis, comparative legal study, and case law examination from Buddhist-influenced jurisdictions, the paper explores ethical and legal innovations inspired by Buddhism. It argues that integrating Buddhist ecological wisdom into environmental law can strengthen normative foundations of sustainability, advance ecological justice, and enhance long-term environmental stewardship, positioning environmental protection as both a legal obligation and a moral imperative rooted in ethical self-restraint and collective responsibility.

Background and introduction

Modern scientific advancement has significantly expanded humanity’s understanding of the natural world; paradoxically, it has also contributed to unprecedented environmental degradation. Life-sustaining resources such as air, water, and soil are increasingly polluted, threatening ecological balance and human survival. This crisis is evident globally, as rapid industrialisation, infrastructure expansion, and unsustainable resource exploitation place severe pressure on ecosystems and local communities.

The scale of environmental degradation reveals the extent to which human activity has disrupted natural systems. Accelerating biodiversity loss has pushed numerous plant and animal species toward extinction, while large-scale deforestation has resulted in soil erosion, declining fertility, and weakened ecological resilience. The widespread use of chemical fertilisers, pesticides, and herbicides has further destabilised soil ecosystems and agricultural sustainability. Compounding these challenges, climate change—manifested through rising global temperatures, sea-level rise from melting polar ice caps, and ozone depletion—poses serious risks to public health and the survival of vulnerable coastal and island populations, underscoring the urgent need for effective environmental governance.

Despite the growth of environmental law through international treaties, national legislation, regulatory institutions, and judicial interventions, its effectiveness remains limited. Predominantly anthropocentric and utilitarian legal frameworks continue to prioritise short-term economic interests over long-term ecological integrity, often treating nature as an object of exploitation rather than a system of which humans are an integral part.

From a Buddhist perspective, environmental degradation is not merely a scientific, technological, or regulatory failure but a moral and spiritual crisis rooted in greed (lobha), ignorance (avijja), and craving (tanha). Buddhist philosophy rejects assumptions of human dominance over nature and instead emphasises interdependence (paticca-samuppada) and impermanence (anicca). Environmental harm thus reflects a deeper ethical and cognitive disconnection from the relational nature of existence.

Buddhist ethical teachings, grounded in the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path, promote values such as non-harm (ahimsa), compassion (karuna), loving-kindness (metta), mindfulness (sati), moderation, and self-restraint. These principles offer a normative foundation for environmental governance by complementing legal regulation with moral responsibility. The doctrine of dependent origination, in particular, highlights how ecological harm inevitably rebounds upon human societies through environmental instability, social injustice, and economic disruption.

This study explores how Buddhist ethical principles can enrich contemporary environmental law by challenging anthropocentric paradigms and supporting ecocentric, responsibility-based approaches. By integrating Buddhist ecological wisdom with modern legal frameworks—such as sustainable development, intergenerational equity, the precautionary principle, and emerging rights-of-nature doctrines—the paper highlights the potential for ethical and legal innovations that foster ecological balance, environmental justice, and resilient systems of environmental governance.

Destruction of the earth as a moral and legal inheritance

Humanity has inherited the planet Earth together with its ecosystems—plants and animals, rocks and minerals, seas, rivers, and lakes. From a Buddhist perspective, this inheritance implies ethical responsibility rather than absolute ownership. While modern science has uncovered many of nature’s mysteries, technological advancement has simultaneously generated severe environmental pollution, rendering nature increasingly inhospitable to human existence. Essential and finite natural resources such as air, water, and soil have been polluted to the extent that human survival itself has become uncertain.

Environmental degradation today is a global phenomenon. The scale and severity of ecological damage reveal how human activity, driven by unchecked exploitation and weak regulatory restraint, has exhausted and destroyed natural resources. Plant and animal life are threatened, with many species already extinct. Deforestation has resulted in soil erosion, exposing barren rock surfaces and undermining agricultural sustainability. The indiscriminate use of chemical fertilisers, pesticides, and weedicides has disrupted natural soil bacteria, producing long-term and often irreversible consequences. Scientists warn of global warming, including the inundation of island and coastal civilisations due to melting polar ice caps. The depletion of the ozone layer exposes humanity to dangerous ultraviolet radiation, while toxic waste accumulation and air and water pollution continue to intensify ecological decline.

From a Buddhist ethical standpoint, the present ecological crisis reflects profound consequences for human well-being and collective happiness. It represents unwise human intervention rooted in ignorance (avijja) and craving (tanha). Buddhism identifies such suffering as arising from wrong views and moral decline. In this context, environmental law informed by Buddhist ethics must aim not merely at regulation, but at transforming human intentions and conduct. Although the ecological catastrophe may no longer be fully preventable, its severity can still be mitigated through ethically grounded legal and policy innovations that promote restraint, responsibility, and interdependence.

Deviation from dependent co-origination (Paticcasamuppāda) and environmental governance

Buddhism teaches that human beings are inseparable from nature. The four primary elements—earth (pathavi), water (apo), heat (tejo), and wind (vayo)—are common to both humans and the natural world (Digha Nikaya, PTS, p. 228). Natural forces such as gravity, climatic conditions, and celestial movements directly influence human life. This causal interdependence underscores the Buddhist principle of paiicca-samuppada, which provides a philosophical foundation for environmental law by recognising the interconnectedness of all phenomena.

Modern technological development often seeks to dominate and ‘conquer’ nature, ignoring its inherent capacity for regeneration and limits of resilience. Human activity has exceeded these limits, resulting in widespread pollution and disease. The Buddha’s guidance on environmental cleanliness, as recorded in the Vinaya Mahavagga (PTS, pp. 109–111), demonstrates early regulatory principles for maintaining healthy surroundings. These teachings illustrate that environmental protection is not merely a modern legal concern but an ancient ethical obligation.

Today, the global atmosphere is heavily polluted by industrial, chemical, and nuclear waste. Technological progress, unrestrained by ethical or legal safeguards, contaminates the air essential for life. Buddhism’s recognition of the close relationship between human conduct and environmental health supports the development of legal frameworks that integrate moral accountability with scientific understanding. Modern experiments confirming that plants respond positively to care further affirm the Buddhist view that human attitudes and actions have tangible environmental consequences.

Causal human effects on the environment and legal responsibility

Buddhism views the world as evolving through immeasurable cycles of formation and dissolution, governed by causes and conditions affecting both physical and moral dimensions of existence. Human beings influence the environment not only through physical actions but also through moral or immoral conduct. According to Buddhist texts, unrighteous governance and unethical social behavior result in environmental decline—manifested as droughts, poor harvests, and diminished human vitality—while righteous conduct produces the opposite effects.

The Aggañña Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya, PTS, pp. 74–76) presents a narrative of co-evolution between sentient beings and their environment. As greed and moral decline increase, natural abundance diminishes. This account offers a conceptual framework for environmental law, emphasising that legal systems must address both material exploitation and ethical degeneration. Environmental degradation is thus not accidental but a conditioned outcome of human choices, reinforcing the need for legal accountability grounded in moral causation.

Moral degradation as the root of ecological crisis

The Gaminicanda Jataka (Jataka No. 257) states that agricultural produce loses its vitality when farmers neglect moral obligations. Buddhism consistently affirms that human intentions and actions—physical, verbal, and mental—shape environmental conditions. Consequently, the ecological crisis is not merely a technical or scientific issue but fundamentally a moral and legal challenge. Environmental law informed by Buddhist ethics must therefore integrate moral responsibility into regulatory structures to ensure sustainable coexistence.

Prominence of mind and wrong attitudes in environmental exploitation

Buddhism teaches that the world is led by the mind (cittena niyyato loko). When societies are driven by greed, distorted values, and unethical desire, environmental imbalance follows, resulting in droughts, famine, and suffering (Anguttara Nikaya, PTS, p. 160). The Dhammapada affirms that unwholesome intentions lead to suffering, while wholesome intentions lead to happiness.

Modern materialistic ideologies, reinforced by industrial capitalism, have legitimised excessive exploitation of nature, often at the expense of vulnerable communities and future generations. From a Buddhist legal perspective, sustainable environmental governance requires a fundamental shift in societal values—from domination and accumulation toward restraint, equity, and compassion.

Moderation and the middle way as a legal principle for sustainability

The Buddhist Middle Way offers a practical ethical foundation for sustainable development and environmental law. Greed and egoism, particularly consumerism and prestige-driven consumption, are primary causes of ecological destruction. Deforestation and large-scale industrial exploitation exemplify the failure to recognize nature as an interconnected system governed by causal laws.

Buddhism advocates small-scale, localized economies using appropriate technology that minimises resource depletion. Avoiding gigantism in industry and agriculture aligns with the Middle Way, ensuring that economic development serves human well-being without violating ecological limits. Environmental policies grounded in moderation would yield long-term social and ecological benefits, preventing irreversible damage.

Wastage, contentment, and environmental regulation

Contentment (santutthi) is a key Buddhist value that discourages waste and promotes environmental protection. The Buddha condemned wasteful practices such as the Udumbara khadika method (Anguttara Nikaya, PTS, p. 22), illustrating early principles against resource misuse. Similarly, Buddhist teachings prohibit water pollution, emphasising legal accountability for environmental contamination (Vinaya, PTS, p. 206). These principles resonate with modern environmental regulations aimed at preventing waste, overexploitation, and pollution.

Moral relationship with nature and legal protection of life

The Buddhist ethical system emphasises a moral relationship with all forms of life. The first precept—abstaining from killing—extends moral concern beyond humans to all living beings. The Metta Sutta articulates a universal ethic of compassion that can inform environmental law by recognising the intrinsic value of non-human life.

Early Buddhist regulations prohibiting harm to animals, insects, and plant life demonstrate a legal–ethical framework that respects ecological balance. Modern practices such as pesticide overuse and habitat destruction violate these principles, leading to biodiversity loss and environmental contamination. Buddhist ethics thus provide a compelling foundation for laws protecting ecosystems and species.

Ethical teachings for environmental stewardship

Buddhist teachings advocate the protection of forests, animals, and water resources as meritorious acts. The Buddha rejected violent sacrificial rituals that destroyed animals and trees, promoting non-violent alternatives. Vinaya regulations restricting tree cutting reflect early conservation principles. These teachings highlight the role of law in safeguarding natural resources against exploitation.

Appreciation of nature and environmental well-being

Early Buddhism emphasises appreciation of natural beauty as essential for mental well-being and spiritual development. Forests, rivers, and parks were valued not only aesthetically but also ethically. Protecting such environments contributes to psychological health and social harmony. Environmental law should therefore recognise nature’s role in human well-being, integrating conservation with public welfare.

Ethical change of lifestyle and sustainable legal reform

Buddhism calls for a radical transformation of human lifestyles and values. Environmental degradation results from materialistic worldviews that prioritize short-term gain over long-term sustainability. Unlike ancient Buddhist civilisations that coexisted with nature for millennia, modern societies face global, human-made ecological crises.

No fragmented legal solution can address these challenges. Instead, comprehensive environmental laws inspired by Buddhist ethics must promote moderation, moral responsibility, and spiritual awareness. Such a value-oriented legal framework offers innovative pathways toward a sustainable and harmonious future.

Buddhist ethical foundations and environmental responsibility

Buddhist philosophy is grounded in the Four Noble Truths and operationalised through the Noble Eightfold Path, which collectively guide ethical behavior, mental cultivation, and wisdom. The ethical dimension (sila)—comprising right speech, right action, and right livelihood—discourages exploitation, violence, and irresponsible economic activity, while promoting livelihoods that minimise harm to living beings and natural systems.

The principle of ahinsa (non-violence) extends moral consideration beyond human beings to animals, plants, and ecosystems, reinforcing the idea that nature possesses inherent moral worth. Compassion (karuna) and loving-kindness (metta) cultivate an ethic of care and responsibility toward both present and future generations. Mindfulness (sati) encourages conscious awareness of consumption patterns, production systems, and ecological consequences, aligning closely with sustainability, environmental impact assessment, and responsible governance.

Interdependence and ecological ethics

The doctrine of dependent origination (paticca-samuppada) provides a philosophical foundation for ecological responsibility by asserting that all phenomena arise through mutual conditions and causal relationships. This relational ontology resonates strongly with modern ecological science, systems theory, and environmental economics, all of which emphasise interconnectedness, feedback loops, and planetary boundaries.

By rejecting the notion of human dominance over nature, Buddhist thought challenges the dualistic separation of humans and the environment that underpins much of Western legal theory. Buddhist texts and practices further reflect environmental consciousness, as illustrated by the Buddha’s reverence for the Bodhi tree and the Vinaya rules restricting monastic activities that harm soil, water, forests, and living organisms. These teachings establish an early normative framework for environmental stewardship, conservation, and restraint, predating modern environmental law by centuries.

Environmental Law: Anthropocentrism and its limitations

Modern environmental law has evolved through international instruments such as the Stockholm Declaration (1972), the Rio Declaration (1992), the Convention on Biological Diversity, and the Paris Agreement (2015). While these frameworks recognise environmental protection as a shared global responsibility, they largely conceptualise nature as a resource to be managed for human benefit rather than as a community of life with intrinsic value.

Judicial decisions, including Massachusetts v. EPA (549 U.S. 497, 2007), Urgenda Foundation v. State of the Netherlands (2019), and Leghari v. Federation of Pakistan (2015), demonstrate increasing judicial willingness to address climate change and environmental harm. These cases advance climate accountability and state responsibility, yet they remain rooted in human-centered rights frameworks, emphasising governmental duties toward citizens rather than recognising the inherent rights or legal standing of ecosystems.

Buddhist ethics challenge this anthropocentrism by promoting ecocentrism, relational responsibility, and moral restraint, offering an alternative legal philosophy that frames environmental protection as an ethical duty arising from interdependence rather than merely a regulatory obligation imposed by law.

Buddhist-inspired legal frameworks and case studies

Bhutan: Gross National Happiness (GNH) — Bhutan’s constitutional commitment to environmental protection reflects deeply embedded Buddhist values, particularly through the principle of Gross National Happiness. Article 5 of the Constitution of Bhutan (2008) mandates environmental conservation and sustainable development, requiring the state to maintain at least 60 percent forest cover. This constitutional approach integrates spiritual wellbeing, ecological integrity, and legal accountability, offering a distinctive model of Buddhist-inspired environmental governance that prioritises collective wellbeing over economic growth alone.

Sri Lanka and Thailand — In Sri Lanka, Buddhist monks and civil society organisations have actively engaged in environmental litigation, advocacy, and grassroots activism, particularly in forest conservation, wildlife protection, and opposition to environmentally destructive development projects. Similarly, Thailand’s recognition of community rights over natural resources and monk-led environmental movements—such as tree ordination ceremonies—demonstrate how Buddhist ethics influence legal consciousness, environmental activism, and community-based conservation.

Japan and Environmental Governance — Japan’s environmental governance reflects Buddhist and Shinto values emphasising harmony, balance, and respect for nature. Judicial decisions and administrative practices increasingly incorporate sustainability, precaution, and disaster risk reduction, aligning with Buddhist principles of restraint, impermanence (anicca), and interdependence.

Legal innovations inspired by Buddhist ethics

Buddhist environmental ethics support several emerging legal innovations, including:

•Ecocentric legal frameworks recognising the intrinsic value of nature beyond human utility;

• Rights of nature doctrines, reflected in constitutional and statutory developments in comparative jurisdictions;

• Intergenerational equity, aligning with karmic responsibility and long-term ethical consequences;

• Restorative environmental justice, emphasising ecological restoration, reconciliation, and healing rather than punitive enforcement alone.

These innovations complement existing legal principles such as the precautionary principle, sustainable development, and the public trust doctrine, reinforcing ethical accountability, long-term thinking, and collective stewardship in environmental governance.

Challenges and opportunities in implementation

Integrating Buddhist ethics into environmental law presents challenges, including concerns over secularism, cultural pluralism, political resistance, and economic priorities. Additionally, the diversity of Buddhist traditions and interpretations complicates uniform legal application.

Nevertheless, significant opportunities exist through soft law mechanisms, judicial interpretation, constitutional environmental rights, education, and policy frameworks that incorporate ethical values without imposing religious doctrine. In this context, Buddhist ethics function as a normative and philosophical guide that informs legal reasoning rather than a prescriptive legal system.

Conclusion

This study demonstrates that Buddhist ethical teachings offer a robust philosophical and moral foundation for reimagining environmental law. By emphasising interdependence, non-harm, mindfulness, compassion, and restraint, Buddhism challenges anthropocentric legal paradigms and supports ethical and legal innovations aimed at sustainability and ecological justice.

Integrating Buddhist ecological wisdom into environmental law can strengthen global environmental governance by aligning legal systems with ethical responsibility, long-term stewardship, and planetary wellbeing. Ultimately, sustainability must be understood not only as a legal obligation but as a moral imperative grounded in humanity’s interdependent relationship with the natural world.
