title: Protecting the State, or empowering the State? Sri Lanka’s counter-terrorism test | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 30 October 2026 00:20
-     - 53

By replacing the Prevention of Terrorism Act, Sri Lanka has an opportunity to strengthen national security, constitutional democracy and investor confidence. That opportunity will be lost if exceptional powers are retained without effective safeguards.

Sri Lanka’s economic recovery has reached an important juncture. Real GDP expanded by 4.7% in the first half of 2026, and macroeconomic stabilisation has restored a measure of confidence after the devastating crisis of 2022. Yet, as the World Bank and the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) have emphasised, recovery is not synonymous with durable prosperity. Productivity, investment, employment, household welfare and resilience to external shocks remain pressing challenges.

Against this backdrop, the Government’s proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTB), intended to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) of 1979, deserves scrutiny extending beyond the familiar contest between national security and civil liberties.

The fundamental question is whether Sri Lanka can construct a legal framework that protects its people against genuine threats while strengthening the institutional credibility on which sustainable economic growth depends.

No responsible Government can disregard terrorism. Equally, no democratic Government should assume that granting itself extraordinary powers necessarily makes the country safer. The legitimacy of national security measures depends not only on their stated purpose but also on their precision, proportionality and accountability.

The burden of history

Introduced as temporary legislation in 1979, the PTA became a longstanding instrument of the State’s security apparatus. Its history is associated with allegations and documented instances of arbitrary detention, torture and the suppression of legitimate political activity, particularly affecting minority communities and Government critics.

For the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), the principal constituent of the National People’s Power (NPP), this history carries particular significance. The party’s experience of severe State repression, especially during the late 1980s, formed part of its political identity. Its opposition to oppressive security laws was therefore more than an abstract commitment to civil liberties.

The transition from opposition to Government, however, presents a familiar democratic dilemma: whether political principles survive the acquisition of executive power.

The NPP’s reliance on the PTA in 2024, in the context of investigations into alleged threats against Israeli tourists in Arugam Bay, illustrates this tension. Governments must respond to genuine security concerns, and previous opposition positions cannot substitute for the responsibilities of office. But a party with direct historical experience of exceptional State powers has an especially compelling reason to ensure that its replacement legislation establishes stronger safeguards.

Nor should the Opposition be exempt from scrutiny. The United National Party enacted the PTA, while subsequent Governments pursued replacement legislation, including the controversial proposals of 2018 and 2023. Political actors across the spectrum have participated in, defended or inherited aspects of this legal framework.

Past inconsistency does not invalidate present criticism. Rather, it reinforces a more demanding standard: civil liberties must be defended as constitutional principles, not deployed selectively as instruments of political advantage.

Legal certainty is an economic asset

The central test of counter-terrorism legislation is whether it defines prohibited conduct with sufficient precision to distinguish genuine terrorist activity from lawful political, journalistic, academic and industrial activity.

Lon L. Fuller, in The Morality of Law, identified clarity and consistency as essential attributes of legality. Lord Bingham, in The Rule of Law, similarly stressed that laws must be accessible, intelligible and predictable.

These principles have direct economic significance.

Entrepreneurs need confidence that commercial disputes and business risks will be governed by predictable rules. Investors require assurance that regulatory and judicial decisions will not depend on arbitrary discretion. Workers and trade unions must be able to exercise lawful rights without fearing that industrial action will be misconstrued as a security offence. Journalists and researchers need space to investigate corruption, scrutinise public expenditure and expose institutional failure.

Where criminal prohibitions are vague, the costs extend beyond those directly prosecuted. Uncertainty can discourage investment, weaken competition, reduce the quality of public debate and increase the perceived risk of doing business.

This is especially consequential for Sri Lanka as it seeks export-led growth, foreign capital, technological upgrading and stronger integration into international markets. Legal predictability is not a substitute for sound macroeconomic policy; it is one of the institutional conditions that makes such policy effective.

The IPS’s State of the Economy 2026 underscores the need to move beyond stabilisation towards productivity-led and resilient growth. That transition requires capable institutions, credible rules and public confidence that the law applies impartially.

Safeguards must work in practice

The proposed PSTB contains provisions intended to protect peaceful protest, advocacy, dissent and industrial action. Such recognition is welcome. However, protective language cannot be assessed in isolation from the offences it qualifies, the powers it authorises and the remedies available to those affected.

In its October 2026 assessment, Human Rights Watch raised concerns about the breadth of the terrorism definition, military search and arrest powers, executive detention authority and restrictions affecting fundamental freedoms. Amnesty International likewise acknowledged improvements over earlier drafts while arguing that significant deficiencies remain, including the potential for prolonged detention without charge and inadequate guarantees against arbitrary enforcement. These are substantive criticisms that Parliament should address through examination of the actual text, not dismiss as political opposition or foreign interference.

The distinction between formal safeguards and effective protection is crucial. A person eventually acquitted may nevertheless have lost years of liberty, employment, income and reputation. The presumption of innocence offers little practical comfort if the process itself becomes a punishment.

Roscoe Pound’s distinction between “law in books” and “law in action” captures the problem. The quality of legislation depends not merely on its wording but also on the institutions implementing it: independent courts, competent investigators, access to lawyers, timely trials and effective remedies for abuse.

Sri Lanka should therefore insist on a narrowly defined terrorism offence linked to genuinely terrorist conduct; explicit protection for peaceful political, journalistic, academic and trade-union activity; prompt and meaningful judicial control over detention; and independent investigation of allegations of torture or unlawful arrest.

Military involvement in civilian law enforcement requires particularly strong justification and oversight. Likewise, powers to restrict movement, assemblies or organisations must be subject to clear legal thresholds, independent review and effective avenues of appeal.

Where ordinary criminal law can adequately address an offence, the Government should explain why exceptional powers are necessary. Where extraordinary measures are genuinely indispensable, they should be proportionate, time-limited and reviewable.

The State is not the Government

An underlying conceptual error in this debate is the tendency to conflate the State with the Government of the day.

In a constitutional democracy, the State comprises the institutions and legal order through which public authority is exercised. Governments temporarily administer those institutions; they do not own them. Criticism of a Government is not inherently hostility towards the country, and peaceful dissent is not a threat to constitutional sovereignty.

This distinction matters particularly when a governing party commands a substantial parliamentary majority. The NPP’s electoral mandate gives it authority to govern, but democratic legitimacy also requires respect for institutional checks, independent scrutiny and the possibility of electoral accountability.

Concerns about delayed Provincial Council elections and the pace of institutional reform reinforce the importance of this principle. Devolved representation, legislative oversight and independent adjudication are not administrative inconveniences. They are mechanisms through which power is restrained and citizens retain meaningful avenues to influence public affairs.

It would be premature to equate every delay or contested legislative initiative with authoritarian consolidation. Yet neither should democratic backsliding be assessed solely by whether elections continue to occur. The quality of democracy also depends on whether opposition, scrutiny and constitutional remedies remain effective between elections.

Write the law for the Government that comes next

The most revealing test of the PSTB is whether its provisions would remain acceptable if administered tomorrow by a Government whose political convictions the present Government strongly opposed.

Would a journalist investigating powerful interests remain protected? Would a trade union be able to organise a disruptive but lawful strike? Would a minority community trust the authorities to distinguish political mobilisation from terrorism? Could a detainee obtain an effective remedy against an unlawful executive order?

These questions are not distractions from national security. They are tests of legislative design.

The Government should undertake meaningful consultation with the legal profession, human rights institutions, journalists, trade unions, minority communities and business representatives. Parliament should scrutinise the Bill clause by clause and revise provisions that fail to meet constitutional and international human rights standards. Independent oversight must be substantive rather than merely administrative, and enforcement must be accompanied by transparent accountability.

The economic case for such safeguards is compelling. Sri Lanka needs investment, innovation, productive employment and public institutions capable of delivering education, healthcare, infrastructure and social protection despite tight fiscal constraints. These objectives cannot be secured by economic incentives alone. They also require confidence that public authority is exercised predictably, impartially and within the law.

A democratic opportunity

Sri Lanka has an opportunity to break with the legacy of the PTA rather than reproduce it under a different name. The Government must demonstrate that national security does not require insulating executive power from scrutiny. The Opposition must apply its principles consistently. Parliament must ensure that the final law is judged by its foreseeable consequences, not its reassuring title.

The ultimate purpose of counter-terrorism legislation is to protect people, their freedoms and the constitutional order against genuine threats. It is not to maximise the coercive capacity of the State.

For a country seeking to transform post-crisis recovery into durable, inclusive prosperity, this distinction is fundamental. Strong institutions, enforceable rights and credible accountability are not obstacles to economic development. They are among its foundations.

A democratic State must be strong enough to confront terrorism and sufficiently restrained to ensure that its citizens do not fear the very law enacted in their name. Sri Lanka’s challenge is not merely to replace the PTA, but to establish a constitutional standard under which national security and human freedom reinforce, rather than undermine, each other.

title: Should Sri Lanka raise income tax-free threshold again? | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 30 October 2026 00:00
-     - 26

By Advocata Institute

Recently, the Government announced a proposal to increase the personal income tax-free threshold from Rs. 150,000 to Rs. 200,000 per month with the upcoming Budget, raises questions about Sri Lanka’s tax policy priorities. While reducing the tax burden on individuals may be justified under certain circumstances, another substantial increase so soon after the previous revision in April 2025 requires a clear justification. At a time when the Government is seeking to strengthen public revenue and increase the contribution of direct taxation, the policy’s implications for the tax base, the distribution of tax relief and fiscal sustainability deserve closer scrutiny.

A narrow tax base

Sri Lanka’s employment-related personal income tax base remains relatively narrow. Published data from the Inland Revenue Department (Table 1 below) indicate that, under the previous tax framework, which had an annual tax-free threshold of LKR 1.2 million, only 24% of registered employees had Advance Personal Income Tax (APIT) deducted in FY 2024/25. These employees accounted for 59% of total gross income earned and paid LKR 191 billion in APIT in total. Although published data on the proportion of employees subject to APIT under the current framework, where the annual tax-free threshold is LKR 1.8 million, are not available, it can be estimated that only around 20% of formal-sector employees are now subject to APIT. These figures do not represent the entire personal income tax base, as they exclude individuals who pay personal income tax through other mechanisms. Nevertheless, they provide an indication of the limited reach of employment-related income taxation in Sri Lanka. 

Table 1: Distribution of Employees, Gross Remuneration and APIT Deductions by Annual Income Bracket, FY 2024/25

This concentration of tax contributions among a relatively small proportion of formal-sector employees raises questions about the implications of further narrowing the personal income tax base. Increasing the annual tax-free threshold from Rs. 1.8 million to Rs. 2.4 million would mean that individuals earning between Rs. 150,000 and Rs. 200,000 per month would no longer be liable for personal income tax, subject to the applicable tax rules. The Government should establish how many taxpayers would be removed from the tax net and how much revenue would be lost before proceeding.

The proposed increase also needs to be considered in the context of the previous reform. In April 2025, the annual tax-free threshold was raised from Rs. 1.2 million to Rs. 1.8 million. The reform also widened the first taxable income band from Rs. 500,000 to Rs. 1 million and removed the 12% tax band. With a further increase now proposed, the Government should explain why such a substantial adjustment is warranted so soon after the previous revision.

One consideration is whether the proposed increase is intended to compensate for inflation or to provide additional tax relief. If the objective is to prevent bracket creep, tax thresholds and bands should be adjusted in line with inflation so that increases in nominal incomes do not lead to higher tax liabilities without corresponding growth in real income. A simple linear projection based on average monthly inflation between March 2025 and September 2026 estimates an inflation adjustment of approximately 12.13% by April 2027[1]. Applying this adjustment to the current monthly tax-free threshold of Rs. 150,000 would raise it to approximately Rs. 168,200. By comparison, the proposed threshold of Rs. 200,000 represents a 33.3% increase. If the inflation estimate is supported by the underlying calculation, this suggests that the proposal would provide relief beyond an inflation-based adjustment, making it important for the Government to justify the additional increase.

Rather than relying solely on a higher tax-free threshold, the Government could also reconsider the structure of the tax bands. Under the current schedule, the first Rs. 1 million of taxable income is taxed at 6%, while the next Rs. 500,000 is taxed at 18%. Reintroducing a 12% band between these rates could create a more gradual progression in marginal tax rates. This would provide an alternative approach to reconsidering the distribution of the tax burden across income levels while retaining the principle of progressive taxation.

The headline tax rate does not tell the whole story

The case for further tax relief should also be assessed by looking beyond the headline tax rates. Under Sri Lanka’s progressive income tax system, individuals pay no tax on income within the tax-free threshold, while income above that threshold is taxed at different rates across successive tax bands. Although the highest marginal tax rate is 36%, it applies only to the portion of taxable income falling within that band, rather than to an individual’s entire income. Consequently, the proportion of total income paid in tax is lower than the highest marginal rate faced by the taxpayer. This distinction is important when assessing the actual tax burden on employees and determining whether a further increase in the tax-free threshold is justified.

The distribution of tax relief also depends on how household income is earned. Unlike many other countries, Sri Lanka taxes individuals separately rather than requiring couples to file joint tax returns as a single household. As a result, two partners earning Rs. 150,000 each per month can have a combined household income of Rs. 300,000 without either exceeding the current monthly tax-free threshold.

Consider a household in which both partners earn Rs. 500,000 per month, giving the household a combined monthly income of Rs. 1 million. Assuming both earn employment income, are taxed separately under the current schedule, and have no additional deductions or reliefs, their combined effective income tax rate would be approximately 18%[YR1] , despite each facing a marginal tax rate of up to 36%. This illustrates how households with relatively high combined incomes can benefit from separate individual tax-free thresholds.

This distinction matters because a further increase in the individual tax-free threshold would provide additional relief to eligible taxpayers regardless of whether they are the sole earner in a household or share household expenses with another income earner. Assessing the proposal solely on the basis of individual incomes could therefore overlook how tax relief is distributed across households with different levels of overall resources.

Who benefits from a higher threshold?

Raising the tax-free threshold is often presented as a way to ease the burden on lower-income earners. However, an increase in the threshold can also reduce the tax liability of existing taxpayers across different income groups, depending on how the tax bands are adjusted. While some lower-income earners may become exempt from income tax altogether, higher-income earners who remain liable for tax may also benefit from paying less.

Under the current tax framework, an individual earning approximately Rs. 233,333 per month would pay around Rs. 5,000 in income tax, equivalent to an effective tax rate of approximately 2.1%. This reflects the tax-free threshold of Rs. 150,000 per month and the 6% rate applied to the next portion of taxable income. Similarly, an individual earning Rs. 1 million per month would pay approximately Rs. 266,000 in income tax, equivalent to an effective tax rate of 26.6%, while facing the highest marginal tax rate of 36%. A higher tax-free threshold could therefore also reduce this individual’s tax liability, depending on how the tax bands are revised. This highlights the need to assess not only the relief provided to those who become exempt from tax, but also the additional tax savings that accrue to existing taxpayers across different income levels.

This does not mean that tax relief is inherently undesirable. Rather, the Government should establish whether raising the threshold is the most effective way to achieve its intended objective. If the primary aim is to support lower-income earners facing higher living costs, the distribution of the resulting tax savings should be examined to determine how much relief reaches those households and how much benefits higher-income taxpayers.

The treatment of employment remuneration and savings is another consideration in assessing the overall tax burden. Employer contributions to the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) and Employees’ Trust Fund (ETF), typically amounting to 12% and 3% of base salary respectively, form part of an employee’s remuneration but are fully exempted from taxation. Income earned within provident funds is also taxed at a preferential rate of 14%, irrespective of the individual’s marginal income tax rate. In contrast, investment income earned outside these arrangements may be taxed at the applicable rate, which can be as high as 36%, depending on the nature of the income and the applicable tax rules.

These arrangements are relevant when assessing the overall tax treatment of employment income and savings. A debate focused exclusively on the personal income tax-free threshold risks overlooking other provisions that already affect the amount of income individuals retain and the tax treatment of their savings.

The fiscal trade-off

Revenue figures for the first half of 2026 highlight the challenge of shifting towards greater reliance on direct taxation. Total Government revenue, including grants, increased by 26% to Rs. 2.955 trillion between January and June 2026, compared with Rs. 2.342 trillion in the same period of 2025. However, income tax revenue, comprising corporate and non-corporate income tax, grew by 16% to Rs. 612 billion. Within this, Pay As You Earn (PAYE) revenue declined from Rs. 76.5 billion to Rs. 74.5 billion over the same period. Meanwhile, Value Added Tax (VAT), which accounted for the largest share of total Government revenue, increased by 22% to Rs. 964 billion.

These figures highlight the differences in growth across revenue categories. While they do not, on their own, establish the fiscal impact of the proposed threshold increase, they underscore the importance of examining the composition of Government revenue alongside its overall growth. VAT revenue grew faster than income tax revenue during the first half of 2026, reinforcing the challenge of strengthening direct taxation as the Government seeks to reduce its relative reliance on indirect taxes. A further increase in the personal income tax-free threshold could complicate this effort if it leads to significant revenue losses that are not offset by improved tax compliance or other revenue measures. Any reduction in personal income tax revenue must therefore be assessed against the Government’s objective of strengthening direct taxation and maintaining its capacity to finance public expenditure.

A higher tax-free threshold would not, by itself, address the problem of individuals and businesses with taxable income remaining outside the tax system. Broadening the tax base also requires effective taxpayer registration, income reporting, compliance and tax administration, including measures to identify taxable income beyond conventional salaried employment. Providing additional relief to existing taxpayers and improving compliance among those who should be paying tax are separate policy questions and should be addressed accordingly.

Broadening the direct-tax base is also relevant to the wider balance of Sri Lanka’s tax system. While taxes on vehicle imports may serve fiscal and other policy objectives, the total tax burden on some vehicles is reported to reach 200% or even 300% of their value. Such high taxes on particular purchases raise questions about the distribution of the overall tax burden, particularly when a relatively small share of formal-sector employees contributes through employment-related income tax. The objective should be to broaden direct-tax participation according to taxpayers’ ability to pay, improve compliance and ensure that revenue is raised through a more balanced and sustainable tax system.

A decision that requires evidence

International comparisons offer some additional context. Sri Lanka’s GDP per capita is approximately $5,002, while its annual tax-free threshold of Rs. 1.8 million is equivalent to approximately 120% of GDP per capita. Countries with similar GDP per capita, including Vietnam, Indonesia, Morocco and Jordan, have different approaches to taxing personal income. While Morocco has an explicit tax-free threshold, Vietnam and Indonesia provide personal deductions or allowances that reduce taxable income but are not directly equivalent to a tax-free threshold. This comparison suggests that Sri Lanka’s current threshold is relatively generous in relation to its income level, particularly given that some economies with similar GDP per capita do not offer an equivalent universal tax-free threshold[2]. This provides a reason to carefully assess the justification for increasing the threshold further.

The Government should therefore publish a clear assessment of the proposed increase before implementing it. This should include the number and income distribution of taxpayers who would benefit, the estimated revenue foregone, the distribution of relief across households and the measures that would be taken to offset any revenue shortfall. The assessment should also explain how the proposal relates to inflation, income growth and the Government’s medium-term revenue strategy.

The question is not whether Sri Lanka should adjust its personal income tax thresholds as economic conditions change, but whether another substantial increase so soon after the April 2025 revision is justified by the available evidence. Given the relatively small share of formal-sector employees contributing through employment-related income tax, the Government should demonstrate that the proposed increase is consistent with its revenue objectives, distributes relief appropriately and forms part of a coherent, sustainable tax policy.

[1] The estimated inflation adjustment is calculated by adding cumulative CCPI inflation of 9.1% between March 2025 and September 2026 to an estimated 3.03% inflation over the subsequent six months. The latter is derived by dividing the cumulative inflation rate of 9.1% by the 18-month period to obtain a simple average monthly rate, then multiplying this by six, assuming no significant changes in price trends. This produces an estimated cumulative inflation adjustment of approximately 12.13% by March 2027.

[2] GDP per capita data for 2025 were obtained from the World Bank Open Data database. Personal income tax-free threshold information for countries with comparable GDP per capita was sourced from PwC’s country-specific tax summaries.

LAHORE: England finally had something to take home when they won the final league match of the Pakistan ODI Tri-Series beating Sri Lanka by 55 runs at the Gaddafi Stadium here on Thursday.

It was England’s first win in four matches having lost their first three and failed to qualify for Saturday’s final where Sri Lanka will meet Pakistan.


With Avishka Fernando, Kusal Mendis and Pavan Rathnayake leading the charge at the top, Sri Lanka looked set to pull off another remarkable chase, much like they did in Rawalpindi. But England kept chipping away at the right moments, broke the key partnerships and eventually secured a win as Sri Lanka chasing 387 was dismissed for 331.

Mendis returning to form made 89 off 71 balls (8 fours, 5 sixes) before falling to Joe Root, caught down the leg side. Janith Liyanage chipped in with 27 off 17, and Sahan Arachchige made 30 off 24. Both stitched together fiery stands with Rathnayake, adding 72 off 38 balls and 57 off 41 balls respectively to keep Sri Lanka in the hunt. Rathnayake smashed 118 off just 77 deliveries (15 fours, 1 six), to keep Sri Lanka in the hunt for as long as he was at the crease. Rathnayake, has scored three ODI hundreds against England this year and two in eight days, but England’s bowlers held their nerve. Once Liam Dawson dismissed him in the 45th over, England wrapped up the game quickly. The left-arm spinner finished with figures of 4/49, emerging as England’s standout performer with the ball.

England, who piled up 429 the last time these two sides met, posted 386-5 after being invited to bat first. Player of the Match Ben Duckett was the star with the bat, registering his highest ODI score with 167 off 132 deliveries (24 fours). The left-hander added 163 runs off 150 balls for the opening wicket alongside Tom Banton (74 off 75 balls, 8 fours, 2 sixes). Harry Brook (44 off 34), Will Jacks (30 off 21), Jordan Cox (43 off 27) and Sam Curran (21* off 12) all chipped in with cameos, but England couldn’t quite produce the blockbuster finish needed to cross the 400-run mark. Asitha Fernando was brilliant with his yorkers at the death, while Dasun Shanaka chipped in with a handy seven-over spell and was the one to break England’s opening stand.

Eshan Malinga went for 101 runs to become only the second Sri Lankan bowler after Nuwan Pradeep to concede more than 100 runs in ODIs. Pradeep gave away 106 runs against India at Mohali in 2017.

title: Sri Lanka’s Asian Para Games campaign: Building on success and investing in future champions | Daily FT
summary:

Medal winners

By Hishan Welmila

Sri Lanka concluded its campaign at the 5th Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, finishing 16th in the overall medal standings with two gold, four silver and three bronze medals. The nine-medal achievement highlighted the country’s continued potential in para-sports, with record-breaking performances and encouraging individual displays providing a foundation for future development.

Distance runner Pradeep Somasiri and athlete Janani Dhananjana emerged as the standout performers for Sri Lanka. Somasiri successfully defended his men’s T46 1,500m title in a Games-record time of 4:03.25, demonstrating his endurance, tactical awareness and ability to deliver under pressure. Dhananjana won gold in the women’s T47 long jump with a Games-record leap of 5.52m and silver in the 200m, confirming her versatility and status as one of Sri Lanka’s leading para-athletes.

Nuwan Indika Gamage secured silver in the men’s T44 100m with a season-best 11.58 seconds, while Palitha Bandara claimed silver in the shot put. Galina Basnayake added silver in the women’s S9 400m freestyle. Bronze medals came from swimmer Naveed Raheem, long jumper Mohamed Safran and 400m runner Maduranga Subasinghe, reflecting contributions from both athletics and swimming.

However, the campaign also brought disappointment. Team captain Samitha Dulan finished fourth in the men’s F44 javelin throw despite his international pedigree, while Dhananjana narrowly missed a medal in the women’s T47 100m before returning to the podium in two other events. These results demonstrate the competitive margins at elite level and the importance of consistent preparation.

Chef de Mission Brigadier (Retired) Dhananjaya Aludeniya highlighted the commitment of the contingent and the need to build on its achievements.

“Our athletes demonstrated remarkable determination, discipline and courage while competing against Asia’s best. Their achievements make us proud, but we must look beyond the medals and recognise the dedication behind every performance. We need to strengthen our support systems, improve preparation opportunities and ensure our athletes receive the resources necessary to reach their full potential,” he said.

Athletics Head of the Contingent Lieutenant Colonel Deepal Herath emphasised the importance of long-term development and identifying future champions.

“Sri Lanka has athletes with considerable potential, and several performances in Nagoya showed that we can compete successfully at the highest level. However, talent alone is not enough. We need scientific training, specialist coaching, regular international exposure and a stronger program to identify young athletes who can represent the country in future competitions,” he said.

Sri Lanka’s performance compares with 11 medals and 18th place at Hangzhou in 2023, and 14 medals and 14th place at Jakarta in 2018. Although the medal tally declined from 2023, the improved overall ranking and two Games records provide reasons for optimism.

Moving forward, investment in sports science, strength and conditioning, rehabilitation, accessible facilities and international competition must become a priority. Equally important is identifying new talent through schools, provincial sports programs, rehabilitation centres and disability organisations. Structured development pathways and opportunities for young athletes to progress into elite competition will be essential.

Sri Lanka’s Nagoya campaign offers both an achievement and a challenge. Sustained investment, stronger coaching structures and a wider talent pool can help convert promising performances into consistent international success and improve the country’s position at future Asian Para Games.

Lionel Messi’s Inter Miami stumbled to a costly 2-2 draw with Cincinnati in a Major League Soccer (MLS) game that sprang to life only after half-time and included four superb goals.

Miami took the lead on Wednesday night with a Luis Suarez strike on the hour mark, but conceded two in quick succession before grabbing back a late equaliser from substitute Riquelme Fillipi to ensure the spoils were shared.

The draw was a setback in Miami’s pursuit of the Eastern Conference’s second seed, as the star-studded side lost ground on the New England Revolution, who beat the New York Red Bulls 3-2.

Despite the heartbreak of Fillipi’s late strike, the point could prove valuable for Cincinnati, who sit on the cusp of the automatic playoff places, but are currently headed for the wild card round and could yet miss out entirely with two games remaining.

In a low-key first half, Miami controlled possession and comprehensively outpassed Cincinnati, but were unable to pierce through.

That changed in the 61st minute, as Rodrigo De Paul picked up the ball in the middle of the park, in acres of space, and played it wide to Casemiro.

The Brazilian played it first time with the outside of his boot to Suarez, lurking just inside the box.

The Uruguayan veteran took one touch, swivelled and perfectly curled the ball into the far top corner, where it crashed down and in off the crossbar.

But Cincinnati rallied, and in the 80th minute Frenchman Kenji Mboma Dem scored with another beautiful curling effort to the far post.

He picked up the ball wide right, ran at multiple defenders with a flurry of stepovers, then cut inside to score.

Just six minutes later, Cincinnati silenced Miami’s Nu Stadium by taking the lead.

Defender Samuel Gidi received a pass on the edge of the box and wrapped his left foot around the ball, sending it past Dayne St Clair.

With Messi heavily man-marked and unable to get a shot away, De Paul sprayed a wide pass to young Brazilian attacker Fillipi, who cut back to the corner of the box and bent it through two defenders and into the far side of the goal.

Both sides had even later chances to win the game, with Suarez blasting his at the goalkeeper before Evander’s shot was blocked by a defender at close range as the referee waved away handball appeals.

Royal Spence Aviation, a partner company of Aitken Spence Travels on Wednesday welcomed a new gateway from Central Asia as Uzbekistan’s Centrum Air launched direct scheduled flights between Tashkent and Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport (MRIA). 

Operating twice weekly, every Wednesday and Saturday, until the end of March 2027, this new service marks another significant step in strengthening Sri Lanka’s air connectivity and tapping into the growing potential of emerging tourism markets.

The new route is facilitated by Royal Spence Aviation, a partner company of Aitken Spence Travels and one of Sri Lanka’s leading airline representation companies, which has been appointed as the General Sales Agent (GSA) and Airport Supervision Agent for Centrum Air; a leading private airline based in Tashkent and a part of Centrum Holding LLC.

At a time when the global travel landscape continues to evolve amid geopolitical uncertainties and shifting travel patterns, the introduction of this service is a timely boost for Sri Lanka’s tourism industry. It reflects the continued efforts of Aitken Spence Travels to diversify the country’s source markets, unlock new visitor segments, and position Sri Lanka as an attractive holiday destination beyond its traditional markets.

Aitken Spence Travels Managing Director Nalin Jayasundera said: “The launch of Centrum Air’s direct service between Tashkent and Mattala is an important milestone in our continued efforts to expand Sri Lanka’s tourism footprint in emerging markets. Uzbekistan and the wider Central Asian region offer considerable untapped potential, and establishing direct air connectivity is a vital step towards converting this opportunity into tangible tourism growth. With the current geopolitical developments reshaping global travel patterns, we believe that strategically developing emerging markets is not simply an opportunity, but a necessity for the long-term resilience of Sri Lanka’s tourism industry.”

Aitken Spence PLC Chairperson Stasshani Jayawardena said: “Strengthening international connectivity is fundamental to Sri Lanka’s tourism growth and competitiveness. This new route not only opens access to a promising emerging market but also creates wider economic opportunity across the tourism value chain. Building these connections is essential as we broaden Sri Lanka’s reach and strengthen our position as a much sought after destination.

For travellers from Uzbekistan, the new service brings the tropical charm of Sri Lanka within easier reach. From sun kissed beaches and thrilling wildlife encounters to mist-covered mountains, ancient heritage sites, and the warmth of Sri Lankan hospitality, the island offers a world of experiences for travellers seeking leisure, adventure, and cultural discovery.

Centrum Air Head of Network Planning Clive Sahamal Fernando said: “The launch of our scheduled direct services between Uzbekistan and Sri Lanka marks an important milestone in Centrum Air’s network development and strengthens air connectivity between our two countries. We see strong potential to expand travel opportunities in tourism, business, and trade, while bringing the people and cultures of Uzbekistan and Sri Lanka closer together. We are grateful to the Sri Lankan authorities and all our partners for their cooperation and support in making this service possible. We look forward to building a strong, long-term partnership and creating new opportunities for connectivity, tourism, and economic cooperation between our two countries.”
